name: Chola Empire
info: The Tamil empire of the Imperial Cholas, founded by Vijayalaya in 848 in the Kaveri valley, which under Rajaraja I and Rajendra I ruled southern India and raided Srivijaya across the sea.

facts.capital: Thanjavur, then Gangaikonda Cholapuram (built by Rajendra I); Urayur and Kaveripattinam were the early Cholas' capitals
facts.founder: Vijayalaya, a descendant of the Early Cholas
facts.predecessor: Pallava and Pandyan dynasties; the Early Cholas of the Sangam literature

t: Vijayalaya founded the Chola Empire in 848, and the Cholas held peninsular India south of the Tungabhadra River as one state between 907 and 1215.
Rajendra I reached the Ganges, built a new capital called Gangaikonda Cholapuram, and in 1025 launched naval raids on the ports of Srivijaya.
The empire declined after Kulothunga Chola III's defeat by Maravarman Sundara Pandiyan II in 1215–16 and ceased to exist by 1279, absorbed by the Pandyan empire.
dyk: According to the Malay chronicle Sejarah Melayu, the rulers of the Malacca sultanate claimed descent from the kings of the Chola empire.
ev: Aditya I defeats the Pallava and Pandyan dynasties, capturing Tondaimandalam and Kongu Nadu
The Cholas send the first of three diplomatic missions to China
Rajendra Chola I launches naval raids on the ports of Srivijaya
Kulothunga Chola I takes the throne after Athirajendra Chola's assassination, beginning the Later Chola dynasty
The Cholas under Kulothunga Chola III help the Hoysalas defeat the Western Chalukyas
Kulothunga Chola III is defeated by Maravarman Sundara Pandiyan II
The Chola state ceases to exist, absorbed by the Pandyan empire

sections.foundation:
The Cholas were among the Three Crowned Kings of Tamilakam with the Chera and Pandya. They appear in the Ashokan Edicts as neighbours of the Maurya Empire, and the Sangam literature names early kings such as Karikala and Kocengannan, with Urayur as their oldest capital. After the Sangam age, around 300, the Kalabhras displaced the Tamil kingdoms, and the Cholas, reduced to chieftains, migrated to Telugu country, where Telugu Chola families claimed descent from Karikala Chola.

In the second quarter of the ninth century Vijayalaya, of the Pottapi Chola family, re-established the dynasty as independent rulers; the Chola Empire was founded in 848. His successor Aditya I defeated the Pallava and Pandyan dynasties early in the 10th century, capturing Tondaimandalam and Kongu Nadu, and Aditya's son Parantaka I defeated the Rashtrakuta dynasty in the battle of Vallala and the Pandyas again. The heartland was the fertile valley of the Kaveri River.
sections.socioeconomy:
The Chola country lay in the flat plain of the Kaveri and its tributaries, now the districts of Thanjavur, Tiruchirapalli, Tiruvarur, Nagapattinam and others. The river, also called the Ponni (Golden) river, had a special place in Chola culture, and its annual floods were celebrated as Adiperukku. Kaveripoompattinam near the delta and Nagappattinam were the major ports, which Ptolemy knew; they drew traders and several faiths, including Buddhism, and Roman coins of the early centuries CE have been found near the delta.

The other major towns were Thanjavur, Uraiyur and Kudanthai, now Kumbakonam; Thanjavur lost its importance after Rajendra Chola moved the capital to Gangaikonda Cholapuram. The Chola raids on Srivijaya had large consequences for trade: Tamil traders entered the realm traditionally controlled by Malay traders, and the influence of the Tamil guilds grew on the Malay Peninsula and the north coast of Sumatra.
sections.military:
Under Rajaraja I and his successors the empire became a military power in South and Southeast Asia. Rajaraja I's naval campaigns captured Sri Lanka, the Maldives and the Malabar Coast. Rajendra I conquered Odisha and the Pala dynasty of Bengal, reached the Ganges, completed the conquest of Rajarata in Sri Lanka, and in 1025 launched naval raids on Srivijaya and the Burmese kingdom of Pegu; an inscription says he captured or plundered 14 places, identified with Palembang, Tambralinga and Kedah among others. Virarajendra Chola later conquered Kedah. The invasions meant to plunder, not to rule, but they gravely weakened Srivijayan hegemony.

On land the Cholas dominated the Western Chalukyas by war and tribute, fought the Eastern Gangas of Kalinga and the Sinhala kings of Rohana, and from 1150 faced constant warfare with the Pandyas. Kulothunga Chola III defeated Hoysala generals at Karuvur and helped the Hoysalas end the Western Chalukyas between 1185 and 1190.
sections.governance:
The empire was ruled by a hereditary dynasty whose line changed in 1070, when Athirajendra Chola was assassinated in a civil disturbance and Kulothunga Chola I, son of the Eastern Chalukya prince Rajaraja Narendra and the Chola princess Ammanga Devi, took the throne, beginning the Later Chola dynasty. Marital alliances bound the Cholas to the Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi, which remained largely independent under Chola protection, and Kulothunga Chola III allied with the Hoysala Veera Ballala II through a marriage.

Feudatories such as the Telugu Cholas of Velanati and Nellore held the eastern coast for the Cholas, aided their campaigns and levied tribute on the Kannada kingdoms. The Cholas were followers of Hinduism and were not swayed by Buddhism and Jainism as the Pallava and Pandya kings had been. Under Rajadhiraja II and Kulothunga III the succession grew murky with disputes and intrigues.
sections.impact:
Under the Cholas the Tamil country reached new heights in art, religion, music and literature; temples and sculpture in stone and bronze reached a finesse never before achieved in India. The Brihadeeswarar Temple was built under Rajaraja I and the chariot-shaped Airavatesvara Temple at Dharasuram under Rajaraja Chola II. The era was a golden age of Tamil literature: Kamban flourished under Kulothunga III, Jayamkondar wrote the Kalingattuparani, Nambi Andar Nambi arranged the Shaivite canon into eleven books, and the Periapuranam, the Virasoliyam and the Nannul were written.

The conquest of Kadaram and Srivijaya and continued contact with China let the Cholas influence the cultures of Southeast Asia; the temple complex at Prambanan shows similarities with South Indian architecture. Rulers of Malacca claimed Chola descent, and princes in Malaysia still bear names ending in Cholan or Chulan, such as Raja Chulan of Perak.
sections.decline:
Around 1118 the Cholas lost Vengi to the Western Chalukyas and Gangavadi to the Hoysala Empire, setbacks soon reversed by Vikrama Chola. The empire was still largely intact under Rajaraja Chola II (1146–1175), and stable and prosperous until 1215 under Kulothunga Chola III, the last great Chola monarch. The decline began with his defeat by Maravarman Sundara Pandiyan II in 1215–16, after which the Cholas also lost Lanka to a revival of Sinhala power.

The Pandyan dynasty rose again as the most powerful rulers in South India, and a Pandyan civil war drew in the Cholas and Sinhalas by proxy, as the Mahavamsa and the Pallavarayanpettai Inscriptions record. The rule of the later Cholas down to the last emperor, Rajendra Chola III, was weaker than before, and the Cholas were absorbed by the Pandyan empire and ceased to exist by 1279.

summary: The Imperial Cholas, refounded by Vijayalaya in 848, made the Kaveri delta the centre of an empire that united southern India and sent fleets against Sri Lanka, the Maldives and Srivijaya. Their reign was a golden age of Tamil temples, bronzes and literature, and their power faded after 1215 until the Pandyas absorbed them by 1279.

pointDescs.848: Vijayalaya founds the Chola Empire, re-establishing the dynasty as independent rulers.
pointDescs.907: From this year the Cholas hold peninsular India south of the Tungabhadra as one state; Aditya I has defeated the Pallavas and Pandyas.
pointDescs.1016: Under Rajendra I, conqueror of Odisha and the Pala lands, the first of three missions goes to China.
pointDescs.1025: Rajendra Chola I's naval raids on Srivijaya and Pegu mark the height of Chola power.
pointDescs.1033: Rajendra I sends the second of three diplomatic missions to China, at the height of the empire.
pointDescs.1070: Athirajendra Chola is assassinated and Kulothunga Chola I begins the Later Chola dynasty.
pointDescs.1118: The Cholas lose Vengi and Gangavadi for a time before Vikrama Chola recovers them.
pointDescs.1146: Rajaraja Chola II begins his reign over a still largely intact empire.
pointDescs.1190: Kulothunga Chola III has helped the Hoysalas defeat the Western Chalukyas in the wars of 1185 to 1190.
pointDescs.1215: Kulothunga Chola III's defeat by Maravarman Sundara Pandiyan II begins the decline.
pointDescs.1218: Kulothunga Chola III's reign ends; the later Cholas are weaker and lose Lanka.
pointDescs.1279: The Cholas are absorbed by the Pandyan empire and cease to exist.

notes: The article's later-Chola dates conflict (rule 'between 1218, starting with Rajaraja Chola II' vs Rajaraja II 1146–1175; Kulothunga III 1178–1218 and stability 'until 1215'); I used 1215–16 for the defeat and 1218 for the end of his reign. The article's Citations and General sources sections are empty in the saved text, so references are []. Administration section of the article is thin (territory only); governance written from dynastic and feudatory material. The 2022 film-industry claim about the Cholas' religion left out as a modern controversy.
